sentences.text: Iberodactylus possessed an estimated wingspan ranging from 375 to 404 centimeters, with wings measuring approximately 4 meters in width.

The preserved skull fragment measures 198 millimeters in length and 128 millimeters in height, featuring a triangular crest with a bone wall about 1.5 millimeters thick. The front edge of this crest on the premaxilla is positioned at an angle of roughly 80 degrees.
The upper jaw bears at least eight conical teeth.
When first discovered, the fossil represented the most complete pterosaur find in Spain aside from Prejanopterus.
Iberodactylus was the largest pterosaur known from the Iberian Peninsula until 2019.
Amateur paleontologist Javier Andreu discovered the skull of Iberodactylus at the Los Quiñones site near Obón in Aragón in the late 1980s.
The holotype specimen was found in the Barremian-aged chalkstone layers of the Blesa Formation.

The species Iberodactylus andreui was formally named and described in 2019 by a team including Borja Holgado and Alexander Wilhelm Armin Kellner. The genus name combines a reference to Iberia with the Greek word for 'finger', while the specific name honors the discoverer, Javier Andreu.
Researchers assumed the specimen was male because the robust crest is considered a plausible display structure.
Holes found on the crest were suggested to be tunnels made by bone-eating beetle larvae.
Iberodactylus is classified as a pterodactyloid pterosaur within the clade Anhangueria. It belongs to the suborder Pterodactyloidea and is part of the unranked group Pteranodontoidea.
Phylogenetic analysis recovered Iberodactylus as the sister species of Hamipterus, placing it in the clade Hamipteridae within the Anhangueria.
Iberodactylus lived between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago during the Barremian stage.
This creature inhabited the region of modern-day Spain.
